source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.address: 2151 Mission College Blvd, Santa Clara, CA 95054
profile.reading: Per Evocative own site, this Santa Clara, California facility (SJC11) sits at 2151 Mission College Blvd and totals 73,000 square feet, with 9 MW of total power capacity delivered as two 4.5 MW feeds from diverse substations. Evocative's own page for SJC11 further describes 2 x 1,200 ton Baltimore Air Coil cooling units with 4 x 75 horsepower pumps, a 5 x 750 kVA UPS system in an N+1 design, and 4 x 1.5 MW Caterpillar generators backing the facility. The operator's own page states this building was originally an Intel network operations center and satellite facility that has since been completely updated for colocation use. The operator lists compliance with HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, ISAE 3402, SSAE 18, LEED, and Green Globes standards, and describes direct fiber connectivity to San Francisco along with multiple carrier options including AT&T, Lumen, Cogent, and Verizon, serving a population of roughly 11.9 million people within 100 miles. Evocative describes itself as a global infrastructure provider operating data center, bare metal, network, cloud, and managed services across 24 data centers in 14 metros, with this Santa Clara building one of two Evocative facilities in the South Bay alongside a separate SJC14 building. Santa Clara, California is headquarters to Intel Corporation and sits at the center of Silicon Valley's dense data center and technology corridor, alongside major colocation campuses operated by Equinix, Digital Realty, and CoreSite in the same city. The area draws power from Silicon Valley Power, the city owned municipal utility, and from Pacific Gas and Electric in surrounding areas, both interconnected to the CAISO grid that also serves much of central and northern California. Evocative, a national colocation operator, has built part of its portfolio through acquisitions of smaller regional colocation operators, consolidating facilities like this former Intel site into a unified network branded under the Evocative name.

reading.body:
The operator publishes 9 MW of total power capacity but no IT load figure, making it impossible to estimate this facility's AI hosting density or compare it to other compute sites by that metric alone.

SJC11 occupies 73,000 square feet of technical space split across two 4.5 MW feeds from separate substations. Floor area signals physical scale but does not determine capacity for AI workloads. Power density per square foot varies widely by facility design and tenant mix, so the square footage alone cannot tell whether this site hosts dense GPU clusters or sparse colocation racks. The dual-feed architecture suggests redundancy and resilience, which matters for uptime but not for the compute capacity question.

The six certifications, including SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, and HIPAA, qualify the facility for regulated workloads in payments, healthcare, and financial services. They attest to audited controls and compliance infrastructure. None of them measure power density, cooling capacity, or suitability for the sustained high heat and electrical draw that GPU-scale AI training requires. Compliance and compute capability are orthogonal.

Among California's 103 mapped data center facilities in this dataset, only five publish a megawatt figure at all, totaling 170 MW. SJC11's published power places it in the sixth position statewide, but that ranking is nominal because it falls outside the five facilities that publish any power data. Within the Santa Clara County cluster, SJC11 is a mid-scale colocation asset whose relevance to AI infrastructure depends entirely on specifications the operator has chosen not to disclose.
